findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The query is built by interpolating owner_id directly into SQL. If owner_id is attacker-controlled, this is SQL injection: the attacker can read, modify, or delete any data the cursor's database user can access. Use a parameterized query and pass owner_id as a bind parameter.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies owner_id such as ' OR '1'='1' --, causing the query to return all orders or execute injected SQL statements, leading to unauthorized data access or modification.
findings.title: Parameterize owner_id in load_order_rows SQL query

findings.body: The loop begins at 1, so entries[0] is never scored or included in the returned list. This drops the first invoice from the ranking.
findings.failure_scenario: When entries has at least one item, the first entry is omitted from the result, so the highest-priority invoice may be missing.
findings.title: Start ranking loop at 0

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default `events=[]` is created once and shared across all calls. The function also mutates the caller's list when one is passed.
findings.failure_scenario: A second call without an explicit events argument reuses the same list, so the previous event_type is still present and the returned dict contains stale events.
findings.title: Avoid mutable default argument
